Front: dream: transcription, part of speech, core meaning?
Back: dream /driːm/ n./v. Noun: a dream, an ambition. Verb: to dream, to have an ambition. The handout says context tells you which sense is meant.
Examples: Goodnight. Sweet dreams. | A bedtime wish: sleep well and have pleasant dreams.

Front: What can follow dream of / dream about?
Back: sb/sth (to dream about somebody or something) or doing sth (to dream or hope to do something).
Examples: She dreamed of/about becoming a chef. | Her ambition was to become a chef.

Front: How is dream that used?
Back: dream that + clause. The word that can be left out: I dreamt (that) I got the job.
Examples: She dreamed that one day she would be famous. | She hoped that one day she would be famous.

Front: What does daydream about mean?
Back: To let your mind wander in the daytime, to fantasise. Keep it apart from the ambition sense of dream.
Examples: daydream about | to daydream, to fantasise (p1)

Front: Three ways to ask about somebody's age?
Back: How old is ...? / What's ... age? / What age is ...? Answer with ... is <number> years old. or His age is <number>.
Examples: He is eight (years old). / His age is eight. | He is eight years old.

Front: How do you say 'at the age of ...'?
Back: at the age of + number, or at age + number.
Examples: In Britain, schooling starts at age 5. | In Britain children start school at the age of five.

Front: How does the handout express 'friends the same age'?
Back: noun + of one's own age, for example friends of their own age.
Examples: Kids need friends of their own age to play with. | Children need friends of the same age to play with.

Front: The two extended meanings of age?
Back: A historical era or period, and a very long time (for ages).
Examples: We are living in the age of technology. | We live in the age of technology. / I've been waiting for ages. | I have been waiting for a very long time.

Front: channel: core meaning and the capital-letter rule?
Back: A sea channel. the Channel = the English Channel, and the capital C is obligatory. Lower-case channel is just the ordinary noun.
Examples: the Channel = the English Channel | The sea between England and France (p2)

Front: Four extended meanings of channel?
Back: Duct or waterway (drainage/irrigation channels), fairway (narrow channel), customs lane (the green channel), TV channel (the Disney Channel).
Examples: If you have nothing to declare, go through the green channel. | At customs, use the green lane if you have nothing to declare.

Front: Which word is channel easily confused with?
Back: Chanel, the luxury brand. The two words are one letter apart, so watch the spelling.
Examples: Chanel vs channel | one letter apart (p3)

Front: The past forms of throw?
Back: threw - thrown, never 'throwed'.
Examples: She threw the bottle into the sea. | She tossed the bottle into the sea.

Front: throw sth to sb or throw sth at sb?
Back: to stresses the direction, at stresses the target. throw sb sth is the double-object pattern.
Examples: He threw his shirt to me. = He threw me his shirt. | He tossed his shirt in my direction.

Front: Which preposition goes with throw to mean 'into'?
Back: throw sth into ...; into stresses the idea of 'going in'.
Examples: She threw the bottle into the sea. | She tossed the bottle into the sea.

Front: What is the core idea of of?
Back: A link between two things - not simply the Chinese possessive word.
Examples: He'd been dreaming of her. | He kept dreaming about her.

Front: What is the core idea of from?
Back: Leaving a starting point and setting off, away from.
Examples: She began to walk away from him. | She started to walk away from him.

Front: What is the core idea of in?
Back: Inside, within a frame or a container.
Examples: I got stuck in a traffic jam for half an hour. | I was stuck in a traffic jam for half an hour.

Front: What is the core idea of on?
Back: On top of, making contact with a surface.
Examples: Be quiet – let me concentrate on my homework. | Be quiet, let me give my full attention to my homework.

Front: What is a verb + preposition called and how does it behave?
Back: A phrasal verb. The unit works like a transitive verb, so an object can follow directly, and a verb after a preposition takes -ing.
Examples: She dreamed of becoming an actress. | Her ambition was to become an actress.

Front: What does consist of mean?
Back: To be made up of.
Examples: Breakfast consists of bread and milk. | Breakfast is made up of bread and milk.

Front: What does hear of mean?
Back: To hear about, to know of somebody.
Examples: Have you heard of her? | Do you know about her?

Front: Two frequent verb + from patterns?
Back: benefit from (to gain from) and suffer from (to be troubled by an illness or pain).
Examples: Many thousands have benefited from the new treatment. | Tens of thousands have gained from it. / She's suffering from back pain. | She is troubled by back pain.

Front: believe in and fill in - what do they mean?
Back: believe in: to trust, to have faith in. fill in: to complete a form.
Examples: My son believes in Santa Claus. | My son has faith in Father Christmas. / Please fill in this application form. | Please complete this application form.

Front: call on and focus on - what do they mean?
Back: call on: to visit somebody. focus on: to concentrate on something.
Examples: Let's call on Kate on the way home. | Let's visit Kate on our way home. / Focus on your own problems. | Give your attention to your own problems.

Front: Give an example where the verb means the same with or without the preposition.
Back: He fought the enemy. = He fought against the enemy.
Examples: He fought the enemy. | He fought against the enemy.

Front: What pattern is pay attention to?
Back: Verb + noun + preposition. An adjective can be added before the noun: pay close attention to, pay scant attention to.
Examples: Pay attention to what the teacher says. | Listen carefully to what the teacher says.

Front: How do the tenses divide around 'and' in the text?
Back: Before and: the background action in progress, past continuous. After and: the point of the sentence, a single finished action, past simple.
Examples: Last year, we were travelling across the Channel and Jane put a piece of paper into a bottle.

Front: Which sentence of the text is past continuous, and why?
Back: we were travelling across the Channel - it sets the background and shows an action in progress.
Examples: Last year, we were travelling across the Channel. | We were crossing the English Channel.

Front: Why does 'Both girls write to each other regularly now.' take the present simple?
Back: The time markers now and regularly point to a present habit; both takes a plural noun and a plural verb.
Examples: Both girls write to each other regularly now. | The two girls now write to each other at regular intervals.

Front: Why is 'However, they have decided to use the post office.' in the present perfect?
Back: It stresses the effect on the present: they no longer send letters in bottles.
Examples: However, they have decided to use the post office. | Even so, they have made up their minds to use it.

Front: Which sentence of the text uses the future simple?
Back: Letters will cost a little more, but they will certainly travel faster. - it states what is very likely to happen.
Examples: Letters will cost a little more, but they will certainly travel faster. | A little dearer, but certainly faster.

Front: What is special about cost?
Back: Its subject is a thing: sth cost sb + money. a little more and faster are the comparatives of much and fast.
Examples: Letters will cost a little more. | Letters will cost slightly more.

Front: What is Jane in 'My daughter, Jane, never dreamed ...'?
Back: An appositive to My daughter: it gives the daughter's name and is set off by commas.
Examples: My daughter, Jane, never dreamed of receiving a letter from a girl of her own age in Holland.

Front: What is the synonym of receive a letter from?
Back: hear from - to get a letter from somebody.
Examples: I used to hear from my best friend. | I used to get letters from my best friend.

Front: Official name of Holland, its adjective and its words for the people?
Back: The official name is the Netherlands (Holland is the everyday name). Adjective: Dutch. One person: a Dutchwoman / a Dutchman. The people as a whole: the Dutch.
Examples: The Netherlands / Holland | the official name is the Netherlands (p4-p5)

Front: What does the handout mark on letter, bottle and little?
Back: /flap t/ - between two vowels the t / tt becomes a light American flap. The same image gives /ˈdɔːtər/ for daughter.
Examples: letter / bottle / little | all marked /flap t/ (p7)

Front: What is the (w) between into and a?
Back: An intrusive sound: a light /w/ is inserted, so into a bottle is read into-(w)-a bottle.
Examples: ... address on it // into a bottle | p7 pronunciation image

Front: What does // mean in the handout's pronunciation images?
Back: A sense-group pause: ... address on it // into a bottle. Break the breath there.
Examples: address on it // into a bottle | p7 pronunciation image

Front: Transcription and stress of daughter?
Back: /ˈdɔːtər/ - the stress falls on the first syllable, daugh-.
Examples: My daughter, Jane, ... | p7 pronunciation image

Front: First line of the imitation template?
Back: My best friend, ___ (name), never dreamed of receiving a ___ (object) from a ___ (person) of his/her own age.
Examples: My best friend, Mary, never dreamed of receiving an email from a boy of her own age.
